# Utility Classes: A Textbook Chapter for the `util` Package

> **AI assistant load scope (Claude Code, Gemini):**
>
> **Load when:** explaining, teaching, or changing a class in `org.cassandragargoyle.api.util`.
>
> **Do NOT load for:** the `fuzzy`, `log`, or `entity` packages, or the TypeScript `preferences` module.
>
> **Authoritative scope:** a beginner-level explanation of the code. The Java source files and their
> doc comments are the authoritative description of the behavior. Section 9 lists behavior that was
> checked against the code on 2026-10-16 and that may change when the code is fixed.

This chapter explains the package `org.cassandragargoyle.api.util`. It has six small classes. Each
class is a box of tools that the rest of the project uses again and again: reading a number from
text, storing a list in one line, writing bytes as text, counting days, remembering the size of a
window, and finding out which operating system the program runs on.

You need only basic Java: variables, `if`, `for` loops, arrays, and strings. Every new idea is
explained when it first appears.

**What you will learn:**

1. What a **utility class** is and why it has a private constructor
2. How to read a number from text without a crash, with a **default value**
3. How an **escape character** lets you put a separator inside the data
4. How **Base64** turns any bytes into text, with bit shifts and bit masks
5. How a computer decides if a year is a leap year, and how it counts days since year 1
6. How a program remembers settings between two runs
7. How to read real code critically: six real traps that we found in this package

---

## 1. The problem: the same small jobs again and again

Imagine you write a big program. A user types `42` into a text field. You need the number `42`, not
the text `"42"`. Tomorrow you need the same in another window. Next week you need to save a list of
recently opened files. Then you need to know if today is a leap year.

These jobs are small, but they come back all the time. If every programmer in the team writes them
again, the project soon has ten slightly different versions of "read a number from text". Some of
them crash on empty text, some do not. Nobody knows which one to trust.

The answer is a **toolbox**: one place where each small job is written once, tested once, and used
everywhere. In Java, such a toolbox is a **utility class**.

## 2. The basic idea: a utility class

![The six utility classes of the util package: StringUtil, Base64Encoder, DateUtil, PreferencesUtil, OsDetector and SystemUtil, each with some of its static methods; a note says that the constructor is private, so you call StringUtil.toInt and never write new StringUtil](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A utility class has two typical features:

- all its methods are `static`, so you call them on the class: `StringUtil.toInt("42", 0)`
- you cannot create an object of it, because an object would have nothing to store

Look at how [`Base64Encoder.java`](Base64Encoder.java) makes sure nobody creates an object:

```java
public class Base64Encoder
{
	private Base64Encoder()
	{
		throw new IllegalStateException("Utility class.");
	}
```

The constructor is `private`, so code outside the class cannot call `new Base64Encoder()`. The
`throw` is a second lock: even code inside the class, or a trick with reflection, fails at once.
`StringUtil`, `PreferencesUtil`, and `SystemUtil` use the same pattern. `OsDetector` has a private
constructor without the `throw`, and `DateUtil` has no constructor at all, so `new DateUtil()`
compiles. It is harmless, but it is a small inconsistency.

> **Think about it:** `Math` in Java is also a utility class. You write `Math.max(a, b)`, never
> `new Math()`. Can you find another one? (Hint: `Arrays`.)

## 3. Why not copy and paste?

The simplest way to reuse code is to copy it. It works for one day. Then someone finds a bug in one
copy and fixes it, and the other nine copies keep the bug. A utility class has one copy, so one fix
helps every caller. It also gives the job a **name**: `StringUtil.toInt(text, 0)` says what happens
better than eight lines of `try` and `catch`.

The price is that a utility class must be **careful**. Many callers depend on it, so a bug in it
breaks many places at once. That is why section 9 of this chapter is about traps.

## 4. Text tools: `StringUtil`

[`StringUtil.java`](StringUtil.java) is the biggest class of the package, with about 50 methods. We
look at four ideas that you can use in your own programs.

| Method | What it does |
| ------ | ------------ |
| `toInt`, `toLong`, `toDouble`, `toBoolean` | read a number from text, or return a default value |
| `isNullOrEmpty`, `notEmpty`, `safeString`, `firstNotEmpty` | small checks for `null` and empty text |
| `toString(Collection)`, `fromString(String)` | store a list in one line of text and read it back |
| `split`, `splitAndStrip` | cut text at a delimiter |
| `bytesToHexString` | write bytes as hexadecimal numbers |
| `escapeForXml`, `appendHtmlEscaped` | make text safe for XML or HTML |
| `longHash` | compute a 64-bit hash of a text |
| `levenshteinDistance` | count the edits between two texts (see [Levenshtein.md](../fuzzy/Levenshtein.md)) |

### Step 1: a number from text, with a default value

```java
public static int toInt(final String value, int dflt)
{
	if (value != null)
	{
		try
		{
			return Integer.parseInt(value);
		}
		catch (NumberFormatException e)
		{
			// will return default
		}
	}
	return dflt;
}
```

`Integer.parseInt("forty-two")` throws an exception. Your program would stop. `toInt` catches the
exception and returns the **default value** `dflt` that you choose. This is the **default value
pattern**: when the input is bad, give a safe answer that the caller chose before.

| Input | `StringUtil.toInt(input, -1)` |
| ----- | ----------------------------- |
| `"42"` | `42` |
| `"forty-two"` | `-1` |
| `null` | `-1` |
| `" 7"` | `-1`, because of the space |

> **Watch out:** `toInt` does not remove spaces. `" 7"` is not a number for `Integer.parseInt`. If
> your text comes from a user, call `trim()` first. And `toBoolean` knows only `"true"` (in any
> case): `toBoolean("yes")` is `false`.

### Step 2: a list in one line, with an escape character

You want to save the list `[a;b, c\d, e]` as one line of text. The obvious idea is to join the parts
with `;`. But the first part already contains `;`. When you read the line back, you get four parts
instead of three.

The solution is an **escape character**. It is a special character that says *"the next character is
data, not a separator"*. `StringUtil` uses the backslash `\`:

![toString turns the list a;b, c\d, e into the text a\;b;c\\d;e; where the orange backslashes are escape characters and the green semicolons are real separators; fromString reads the text and returns the same list](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```java
for (String part : parts)
{
	int length = part.length();
	for (int i = 0; i < length; i++)
	{
		char c = part.charAt(i);
		if (c == '\\' || c == sep)
		{
			sb.append("\\");
		}
		sb.append(c);
	}
	sb.append(sep);
}
```

Two characters need an escape: the separator, and the backslash itself. If the backslash had no
escape, the reader could not tell `\;` (an escaped separator) from a real backslash at the end of a
part followed by a real separator.

Reading is the mirror image. `fromString` keeps one flag, `forceNext`:

```java
if (forceNext)
{
	sb.append(c);
	forceNext = false;
}
else if (c == '\\')
{
	forceNext = true;
}
else if (c == sep)
{
	parts.add(sb.toString());
	sb.setLength(0);
}
else
{
	sb.append(c);
}
```

| In the picture | In the code |
| -------------- | ----------- |
| orange `\` | `c == '\\'` sets `forceNext = true` and is not stored |
| the character after an orange `\` | `forceNext` is `true`, so `c` goes into the part |
| green `;` | `c == sep`, the part is finished and added to the list |

You know this idea from Java itself: in `"say \"hi\""` the backslash lets you put a quote inside a
string. JSON, CSV, and URLs use the same trick with other characters.

> **Watch out:** `toString` writes a separator **after every part**, also after the last one.
> `fromString` adds a part only when it sees a separator. So `fromString("a;b")` returns only
> `[a]`. Text that `toString` made always works; text that you type by hand must end with `;`.

**Try it yourself:** Write on paper what `StringUtil.toString(List.of("1;2", "3"))` returns. Check
your answer in exercise 3.

### Step 3: bytes as hexadecimal text

A byte has 8 bits, a value from 0 to 255. **Hexadecimal** (base 16) writes it with two digits from
`0123456789abcdef`. Each digit stands for 4 bits, a **nibble**.

```java
for (int b : bytes)
{
	b &= 0xff;
	sb.append(HEXDIGITS[b >> 4]);
	sb.append(HEXDIGITS[b & 15]);
	sb.append(cDelim);
```

- `b &= 0xff` fixes the sign. A Java `byte` is from -128 to 127, so the byte `0xCA` arrives as `-54`.
  `& 0xff` keeps only the lowest 8 bits and gives `202` again
- `b >> 4` moves the bits 4 places to the right: the high nibble. For `202` (`1100 1010`) it is `12`, `c`
- `b & 15` keeps the lowest 4 bits: the low nibble. For `202` it is `10`, `a`

`bytesToHexString(new byte[] {(byte) 0xCA, (byte) 0xFE, 0x0A, (byte) 255}, ' ', 0)` returns
`"ca fe 0a ff "`. With a line length above 0, it adds one more delimiter after every 8 bytes and a
new line after `nLineLen` bytes, like the output of a hex editor.

### Step 4: a hash of a text

A **hash** is a number computed from data. Equal texts always give equal hashes, so you can compare
two hashes instead of two long texts.

```java
public static long longHash(String value)
{
	long h = 1125899906842597L;
	int len = value.length();
	for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
	{
		h = 31 * h + value.charAt(i);
	}
	return h;
}
```

This is the same formula as `String.hashCode()` in Java, with two changes: it uses a 64-bit `long`
instead of a 32-bit `int`, and it starts from a big prime number instead of 0. More bits mean fewer
**collisions** (two different texts with the same hash).

> **Watch out:** fewer is not zero. `"Aa".hashCode()` and `"BB".hashCode()` are both `2112`, and
> `longHash("Aa")` and `longHash("BB")` are also equal (`1081989810475737829`). The reason: `'A'` is
> 65 and `'a'` is 97, `'B'` is 66. So `31·65 + 97 = 31·66 + 66`. A bigger start number does not
> change that. A hash tells you "maybe equal"; to be sure, compare the texts.

## 5. Bytes as text: `Base64Encoder`

E-mail, JSON, and web addresses were made for text. A photo or a key file is **bytes**, and many byte
values are not printable characters. **Base64** writes any bytes with only 64 safe characters:
`A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `+`, and `/`. You meet it every day: e-mail attachments, the images inside the
other textbook chapters of this project, and login tokens on the web.

### The smart idea: 3 bytes are 4 characters

64 is 2⁶, so one Base64 character carries exactly **6 bits**. 3 bytes have 3 · 8 = 24 bits, and 24
bits are exactly 4 groups of 6 bits. So every 3 bytes become 4 characters:

![The bytes of Man, 77, 97 and 110, written as 24 bits, cut into four groups of 6 bits with the values 19, 22, 5 and 46; the table MAP1 turns them into the characters T, W, F and u](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The table that turns a 6-bit value into a character is the array `MAP1`. It is filled once, when the
class loads, in a `static` block:

```java
private static final char[] MAP1 = new char[64];

static
{
	int i = 0;
	for (char c = 'A'; c <= 'Z'; c++)
	{
		MAP1[i++] = c;
	}
```

After the loops, `MAP1[0]` is `'A'`, `MAP1[25]` is `'Z'`, `MAP1[26]` is `'a'`, `MAP1[52]` is `'0'`,
and `MAP1[63]` is `'/'`. A second array, `MAP2`, is the reverse table for decoding: from a character
back to its value, with `-1` for characters that are not in the alphabet.

### Step 1: cut 24 bits into four pieces

```java
int i0 = in[ip++] & 0xff;
int i1 = ip < iLen ? in[ip++] & 0xff : 0;
int i2 = ip < iLen ? in[ip++] & 0xff : 0;
int o0 = i0 >>> 2;
int o1 = ((i0 & 3) << 4) | (i1 >>> 4);
int o2 = ((i1 & 0xf) << 2) | (i2 >>> 6);
int o3 = i2 & 0x3F;
```

Three tools do all the work:

| Tool | Meaning | Example with `'M'` = 77 = `01001101` |
| ---- | ------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `x >>> n` | move the bits n places to the right, the lowest n bits fall out | `77 >>> 2` = `010011` = 19 |
| `x & mask` | keep only the bits where the **mask** has a 1 | `77 & 3` = `01` = 1 |
| `x << n` | move the bits n places to the left, add zeros on the right | `1 << 4` = `010000` = 16 |
| `a \| b` | join the bits of two numbers | `16 \| (97 >>> 4)` = `16 \| 6` = 22 |

| In the picture | In the code |
| -------------- | ----------- |
| first 6 bits of `M` | `i0 >>> 2` |
| last 2 bits of `M`, then first 4 bits of `a` | `((i0 & 3) << 4) \| (i1 >>> 4)` |
| last 4 bits of `a`, then first 2 bits of `n` | `((i1 & 0xf) << 2) \| (i2 >>> 6)` |
| last 6 bits of `n` | `i2 & 0x3F` |

### Step 2: padding at the end

What if the data has 2 bytes, not 3? The code uses `0` for the missing byte, so the bits still fit.
But the reader must know that the last byte was not real. Base64 marks it with the **padding**
character `=`:

```java
int oDataLen = (iLen * 4 + 2) / 3;       // output length without padding
int oLen = ((iLen + 2) / 3) * 4;         // output length including padding
...
out[op] = op < oDataLen ? MAP1[o2] : '=';
```

| Input | Bytes | Output |
| ----- | ----- | ------ |
| `"Man"` | 3 | `TWFu` |
| `"Ma"` | 2 | `TWE=` |
| `"M"` | 1 | `TQ==` |
| `"Hello"` | 5 | `SGVsbG8=` |

`((iLen + 2) / 3) * 4` is a classic trick: **round up with integer division**. `iLen / 3` rounds
down, so adding `2` first makes it round up. For 5 bytes: `(5 + 2) / 3 = 2` groups, `2 · 4 = 8`
characters.

> **Watch out:** Base64 is **not encryption**. Anyone can decode it, there is no key. It only makes
> bytes safe to send as text.

**Try it yourself:** Encode `"Hi!"` on paper: `H` = 72, `i` = 105, `!` = 33. Write the 24 bits, cut
them into 4 groups, and look up the characters. Exercise 1 has the answer.

The decoder does the same steps backwards and checks its input. A length that is not a multiple of 4,
or a character outside the alphabet (a space, a new line, `-`), throws `IllegalArgumentException`.
Since Java 8, the standard library has `java.util.Base64` with the same output; this class stays for
the code that already uses it.

## 6. Counting days: `DateUtil`

[`DateUtil.java`](DateUtil.java) has helpers for `java.util.Date`: formatting (`formatDate` writes
`dd-MM-yyyy`), `min` and `max` that accept `null`, and two methods that turn a date into a **day
number** and back. A day number is handy: the difference of two day numbers is the number of days
between two dates, and you need no calendar for it.

### Step 1: the leap year rule

A year has about 365.2425 days. To keep the calendar in step with the sun, some years get a 29th
February. The rule has three parts, and the order matters:

![Leap year decision: if year % 400 == 0 it is a leap year; otherwise if year % 100 == 0 it is not; otherwise if year % 4 == 0 it is a leap year; otherwise it is not. Examples: 2000, 2024 and 2400 are leap years, 1900, 2026 and 2100 are not](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```java
public static boolean isLeapYear(int year)
{
	return (0 == year % 400) || ((0 != year % 100) && (0 == year % 4));
}
```

`%` is the remainder of a division. `year % 4 == 0` means "divisible by 4". The whole rule fits in
one line because `||` and `&&` do the "otherwise" for us: if the first part is `true`, Java does not
even look at the rest.

### Step 2: from a date to a day number

Day 1 is 1 January of the year 1. `toDayCount` adds the days in pieces:

```java
// Days in current year
int dayCount = (RG_DAYS[month - 1] + day);
if (month > 2 && isLeapYear(year))
{
	dayCount++;
}

// Days in complete years
dayCount += (365 * (year - 1));
```

`RG_DAYS` is a table of the days **before** each month in a normal year: `0, 31, 59, 90, ...`. For
16 October: `RG_DAYS[9]` is 273 (January to September), plus 16 is 289. The leap day counts only
after February. Then the code adds 365 days for every complete year, and finally the leap days of
the complete years, with the three rules from step 1:

```java
dayCount += ((year / 100) * 24);
dayCount += ((year - 1) / 400);
dayCount += (((year % 100) - 1) / 4);
```

For 16 October 2026: 289 + 365 · 2025 + 20 · 24 + 5 + 6 = **739905**.

> **Watch out:** for the year 2000, `((year % 100) - 1) / 4` is `-1 / 4`. In Java, integer division
> **cuts toward zero**, so the result is `0`, not `-1`. The code depends on this. In Python, `-1 // 4`
> is `-1`. If you copy integer arithmetic between languages, check negative numbers.

### Step 3: from a day number back to a date

`fromDayCount` goes the other way. It does not try every year. It **peels off big pieces first**,
the way you turn 7384 seconds into hours, minutes, and seconds:

| Piece | Days | Why |
| ----- | ---- | --- |
| 400 years | 146097 | 400 · 365 + 97 leap days; after 400 years the calendar repeats exactly |
| 100 years | 36524 | 100 · 365 + 24 leap days (the century year is not a leap year) |
| 4 years | 1461 | 4 · 365 + 1 |
| 1 year | 365 | |

```java
year = (400 * (dayCount / 146097));
dayCount %= 146097;
...
year += (100 * (dayCount / 36524));
dayCount %= 36524;
```

`/` tells how many whole pieces fit, `%` tells what is left. We checked every day from 1601 to 2400:
`fromDayCount(toDayCount(date))` gives the same date back, and the day numbers match
`java.time.LocalDate`. A day number of 0 or less is not an error: it gives 1 January 2100, a value
that the old callers use as "no date".

## 7. Remembering settings: `PreferencesUtil`

A good program remembers your settings: the size of its window, the last opened files, the font
size. Java has a built-in store for this, `java.util.prefs.Preferences`. It keeps **key-value pairs**,
but only simple values: text, numbers, `true` or `false`. [`PreferencesUtil.java`](PreferencesUtil.java)
adds methods for things that are not simple.

### Step 1: a list as many keys

A list does not fit in one key. `putStringList` stores the size under the key itself, and every item
under the key plus its position:

![putStringList with the list a.txt, b.txt, c.txt stores recent=3, recent0, recent1 and recent2; after a second call with x.txt and y.txt, recent=2, recent0 and recent1 change, and the old recent2=c.txt stays but is ignored, so getStringList returns x.txt and y.txt](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```java
int pos = 0;
for (String value : values)
{
	if (value != null)
	{
		prefs.put(key + pos, value);
		pos++;
		...
	}
}
prefs.putInt(key, pos);
```

When you store a shorter list, the old keys at the end stay in the store. That is not a problem,
because `getStringList` reads the size first and stops there. A `Dimension` (width and height) and a
`Rectangle` (x, y, width, height) are stored the same way, as two or four keys with the suffixes
`_dimension_width`, `_bounds_x`, and so on.

### Step 2: do not store the default value

```java
public static void putIntValue(Preferences prefs, String key, int value, int defaultValue)
{
	String old = prefs.get(key, null);
	if (value != defaultValue)
	{
		prefs.putInt(key, value);
	}
	else if (old != null)
	{
		prefs.remove(key);
	}
}
```

If the user sets the font size back to the default, the key is **removed**, not stored. Why? Next
year the programmers may change the default from 12 to 14. A user who never changed the font gets
the new default, because nothing is stored for them. A user who chose 16 keeps 16.

## 8. Where do we run? `OsDetector` and `SystemUtil`

### Step 1: the name of the operating system

Java tells you the name of the operating system in the system property `os.name`, for example
`Linux`, `Windows 11`, or `Mac OS X`. [`OsDetector.java`](OsDetector.java) turns it into one of a
few fixed names:

```java
String os = getOperatingSystemName().toLowerCase();

if (os.contains("win"))
{
	return Constants.PROP_OS_WINDOWS;
}
else if (os.contains("mac"))
{
	return Constants.PROP_OS_MAC;
}
else if (os.contains("nix") || os.contains("nux") || os.contains("aix"))
{
	return Constants.PROP_OS_LINUX_UNIX;
}
```

`isWindows()`, `isLinux()`, and `isMacOS()` compare this result. `getPlatformString()` adds the
processor type from `os.arch` and returns `linux-x86_64` or `windows-x86_64`; on other platforms it
throws `UnsatisfiedLinkError`, because the project has native libraries only for these two.

> **Think about it:** the order of the `if` tests matters. `"darwin"` (the core of macOS) contains
> `"win"`. Java reports `Mac OS X`, so it works today, but a test that is too general can catch the
> wrong case. Put the most specific test first.

### Step 2: run another program

`SystemUtil.execute` starts another program and returns everything it printed:

```java
Process process = Runtime.getRuntime().exec(command);

StreamReader reader = new StreamReader(process.getInputStream());
reader.start();
process.waitFor();
reader.join();

return reader.getResult();
```

Why a separate thread, `StreamReader`? The output of the other program goes through a **pipe** with a
small buffer. If nobody reads the pipe, the buffer fills up and the other program stops and waits.
If your program at the same time waits for the other program to finish, both wait forever. This is a
**deadlock**. The `StreamReader` thread empties the pipe while the main thread waits.

> **Watch out:** `exec(String)` does not use a shell. It only cuts the command at spaces. Quotes,
> `|`, and `*` have no special meaning: `execute("echo 'a b'")` prints `'a b'` **with** the quotes.
> And only the normal output is read, not the error output.

The other methods of `SystemUtil` read a `double` from a system property with a default value (the
pattern from section 4), and read the scale factor and resolution of the screen.

## 9. Traps we found in this code

Real code has bugs, also tested code in a real project. Reading code **critically** is an important
skill. We checked each of these with a small program on 2026-10-16. They may be fixed when you read
this, so check them yourself.

### Trap 1: midnight at noon

![DateUtil.toMidnight sets Calendar.HOUR to 0; Calendar sees 15:30 as HOUR 3 PM, setting HOUR to 0 keeps PM, so 15:30 becomes 12:00; set(Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY, 0) would give 00:00](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

`toMidnight` uses `Calendar.HOUR`, which is the hour on a **12-hour clock**. Setting it to 0 keeps
`AM` or `PM`. So `toMidnight` of 15:30 is **12:00**, not 00:00. The same mistake makes
`atMidnight(12:00)` return `true`, and `isToday` returns `false` for 9:00 today when the clock shows
an afternoon time. The fix is one word: `Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY`.

### Trap 2: a part that is never found

`StringUtil.stringPart("x;y;z", 1, ';')` should return `"y"`. It returns `null`. The variable
`readingNr` counts the parts, but nothing in the method ever increases it, so only part 0 works.
Exercise 7 asks you to fix it.

### Trap 3: Ubuntu that is not Ubuntu

`OsDetector.isUbuntu()` returns `false` on Ubuntu. The file `/etc/os-release` contains
`NAME="Ubuntu"`. `Properties` keeps the quotes, so the value is `"Ubuntu"` **with** quotes and a
capital `U`, and the code looks for `ubuntu` in lower case.

### Trap 4: one process that does not exist

On Linux, `SystemUtil.countRunningProcesses` returns **1** for a program that does not run.
`pgrep` prints nothing, and `"".split("\n")` in Java is an array with **one** empty string, not an
empty array.

### Trap 5: `null` handled in one method, but not in its twin

`endsIgnoreCase(null, "x")` returns `false`, but `startsIgnoreCase(null, "x")` throws a
`NullPointerException`. In the same way, `PreferencesUtil.putValue` throws a `NullPointerException`
when the value is `null` and the default is not, because `Preferences.put` does not accept `null`.

### Trap 6: a shared calendar

`DateUtil` keeps one `Calendar` object in a `static` field and uses it in `toMidnight` and
`atMidnight`. A `Calendar` is not **thread-safe**: two threads that change it at the same time mix up
their values. The code protects it with `synchronized (CALENDAR)`, so only one thread at a time can
use it. The formatter `FastDateFormat` from Apache Commons is thread-safe, so it can be shared
without a lock; the older `java.text.SimpleDateFormat` cannot.

## 10. How fast is it?

| Method | Time | Memory | Example |
| ------ | ---- | ------ | ------- |
| `toInt`, `isLeapYear`, `toDayCount`, `fromDayCount` | O(1) | O(1) | the same few steps for any input |
| `toString`, `fromString`, `escapeForXml`, `longHash` | O(n) | O(n) | one pass over n characters |
| `Base64Encoder.encode` | O(n) | O(n) | 3,000,000 bytes give exactly 4,000,000 characters |
| `levenshteinDistance` | O(n·m) | O(n) | see [Levenshtein.md](../fuzzy/Levenshtein.md) |
| `execute`, `countRunningProcesses` | depends on the other program | the whole output | starting a process takes milliseconds |

O(1) means "the time does not grow with the input". O(n) means "twice as much input, about twice the
time". Base64 output is always about 4/3 of the input, so an image of 30 KB is about 40 KB as Base64.

## 11. The same code in other languages

The `util` package exists only in Java. The other modules use the standard tools of their language:

| Job | Python | Go | TypeScript |
| --- | ------ | -- | ---------- |
| Base64 | `base64.b64encode` | `encoding/base64` | `Buffer.from(...).toString("base64")` |
| number from text with a default | `int(text)` in `try` | `strconv.Atoi` with an error check | `Number.parseInt` and `Number.isNaN` |
| settings | - | - | the [`preferences`](../../../../../../../../typescript/src/preferences/README.md) module |
| operating system | `platform.system()` | `runtime.GOOS` | `process.platform` |

The TypeScript `preferences` module is not a twin of `PreferencesUtil`. It has its own design with
stores and listeners.

## 12. Use it: a small toolbox demo

Save this program as `Toolbox.java` in a folder `org/cassandragargoyle/api/demo/`:

```java
package org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo;

import java.util.Calendar;
import java.util.List;
import org.cassandragargoyle.api.util.Base64Encoder;
import org.cassandragargoyle.api.util.DateUtil;
import org.cassandragargoyle.api.util.OsDetector;
import org.cassandragargoyle.api.util.StringUtil;

public class Toolbox
{
	public static void main(String[] args)
	{
		// 1. Read numbers from text without a crash
		String[] inputs = {"42", "forty-two", null, " 7"};
		for (String input : inputs)
		{
			System.out.println("toInt(" + input + ") = " + StringUtil.toInt(input, -1));
		}

		// 2. Store a list in one line of text and get it back
		List<String> names = List.of("Anna", "Tom;Jerry", "C:\\temp");
		String line = StringUtil.toString(names);
		System.out.println("saved:  " + line);
		System.out.println("loaded: " + StringUtil.fromString(line));

		// 3. Base64 there and back
		String secret = Base64Encoder.encodeString("Hello");
		System.out.println("Base64: " + secret + " -> " + Base64Encoder.decodeString(secret));

		// 4. Dates
		for (int year : new int[] {1900, 2000, 2024, 2026})
		{
			System.out.println(year + (DateUtil.isLeapYear(year) ? " is" : " is not") + " a leap year");
		}
		Calendar cal = Calendar.getInstance();
		cal.clear();
		cal.set(2026, Calendar.OCTOBER, 16);
		System.out.println("16-10-2026 is day number " + DateUtil.toDayCount(cal.getTime()));
		System.out.println("day 1 is " + DateUtil.formatDate(DateUtil.fromDayCount(1)));

		// 5. Where do we run?
		System.out.println("OS: " + OsDetector.getOS());
	}
}
```

Build the project once (`make build-java`), then compile and run the demo from the repository root.
`DateUtil` needs the Apache Commons Lang library from your Maven repository (`~/.m2`), so put it on
the class path too (on Windows, use `;` instead of `:`):

```bash
LANG3=$(find ~/.m2/repository/org/apache/commons/commons-lang3 -name 'commons-lang3-*.jar' | head -1)
javac -cp java/target/classes:$LANG3 -d demo-out org/cassandragargoyle/api/demo/Toolbox.java
java -cp java/target/classes:$LANG3:demo-out org.cassandragargoyle.api.demo.Toolbox
```

Output (on Linux; the last line shows `Windows` on Windows):

```text
toInt(42) = 42
toInt(forty-two) = -1
toInt(null) = -1
toInt( 7) = -1
saved:  Anna;Tom\;Jerry;C:\\temp;
loaded: [Anna, Tom;Jerry, C:\temp]
Base64: SGVsbG8= -> Hello
1900 is not a leap year
2000 is a leap year
2024 is a leap year
2026 is not a leap year
16-10-2026 is day number 739905
day 1 is 01-01-0001
OS: Linux/Unix
```

Look at the line `saved:`. You can see both escape cases: `Tom\;Jerry` and `C:\\temp`.

## 13. Exercises

Try each exercise on your own first, then check your answer in section 15.

**1.** What does `Base64Encoder.encodeString("Hi!")` return? How many `=` characters does the result of
`encodeString("Hello")` have, and why?

**2.** Is 2100 a leap year? Is 2400? Use the three questions from section 6.

**3.** What does `StringUtil.toString(List.of("1;2", "3"))` return?

**4.** What does `StringUtil.toInt(" 42", 0)` return? How would you change **your** code that calls it
so that it accepts the spaces?

**5.** What does `StringUtil.bytesToHexString(new byte[] {0x0F, 0x10}, ':', 0)` return?

**6.** Why does `PreferencesUtil.putIntValue` remove the key when the value is the same as the default,
instead of storing it?

**7.** *(Challenge.)* Fix `stringPart` from trap 2: copy the method into your own class and add the
missing line. Then check that `stringPart("x;y;z", 1, ';')` is `"y"`, part 2 is `"z"`, part 3 is
`null`, and that `stringPart("a\\;b;c", 1, ';')` is `"c"`. Write the checks as a JUnit test.

## 14. Words to remember

| Term | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| Utility class | a class with only `static` methods and a private constructor; you never create an object of it |
| Default value | the safe answer that a method returns when the input is bad |
| Escape character | a character that says "the next character is data, not a command"; here the backslash |
| Base64 | a way to write any bytes with 64 printable characters, 6 bits per character |
| Padding | the `=` characters that fill the last group of Base64 output |
| Bit shift | `<<`, `>>`, `>>>`: move the bits of a number to the left or right |
| Bit mask | a number used with `&` to keep only some bits, for example `0x3F` keeps the lowest 6 |
| Nibble | 4 bits, one hexadecimal digit |
| Hash | a number computed from data; equal data give equal hashes |
| Collision | two different inputs with the same hash |
| Leap year | a year with 29 February: divisible by 4, but not by 100, unless by 400 |
| Deadlock | two parts of a program wait for each other, so neither can go on |
| Thread-safe | can be used by several threads at the same time without a lock |

## 15. Answers

**1.** `"SGkh"`. The bits of `H`, `i`, `!` are `01001000 01101001 00100001`, the 6-bit groups are 18,
6, 36, 33, and `MAP1` gives `S`, `G`, `k`, `h`. `"Hello"` gives `"SGVsbG8="` with **one** `=`: 5 bytes
are one full group of 3 and a group of 2 bytes, and a group of 2 bytes needs one padding character.

**2.** 2100 is not a leap year: it is not divisible by 400, but it is divisible by 100. 2400 is a leap
year: it is divisible by 400.

**3.** `1\;2;3;` (in Java source code you would write it as `"1\\;2;3;"`). The `;` inside the first
part gets a backslash, and every part ends with `;`.

**4.** `0`, the default value, because `Integer.parseInt(" 42")` fails on the space. Call
`StringUtil.toInt(text.trim(), 0)`, and check for `null` first, because `trim()` on `null` throws a
`NullPointerException`.

**5.** `"0f:10:"`. Each byte gives two hexadecimal digits and a delimiter, also after the last byte.
With `nLineLen` 0 there are no line breaks.

**6.** So that a user who never changed the setting always gets the current default of the program.
If the default changes in a new version, nothing old is stored that would hide it.

**7.** In the branch `else if (c == sep)`, increase the counter after the check:

```java
else if (c == sep)
{
	if (readingNr == partNr)
	{
		return sb.toString();
	}
	readingNr++;
}
```

With this line the four checks give `"y"`, `"z"`, `null`, and `"c"`. Part 0 of `"a\\;b;c"` is
`"a;b"`, because the escaped `;` belongs to the data.
